claim: In temperate climates, winter deaths exceed summer ones.
source: In temperate climates, winter deaths exceed summer ones.
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract, supported by citations in the introduction (Campbell, 2017; Fowler et al., 2015; Healy, 2003; McKee, 1989).

claim: Death rates in men and women ≥ 45 years peaked in December to February and were lowest in June to August.
source: Death rates in men and women ≥ 45 years peaked in December to February and were lowest in June to August, driven by cardiorespiratory diseases and injuries.
evidence: This finding is directly stated in the abstract and supported by Figure 11 showing center of gravity analysis results.

claim: Seasonality of all-cause mortality in men and women ≥ 45 years is driven by cardiorespiratory diseases and injuries.
source: Death rates in men and women ≥ 45 years peaked in December to February and were lowest in June to August, driven by cardiorespiratory diseases and injuries.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this causal relationship, supported by cause-specific analysis in Figures 5-7.

claim: Percent difference in death rates between peak and minimum months did not vary across climate regions for ages ≥ 45 years.
source: In these ages, percent difference in death rates between peak and minimum months did not vary across climate regions, nor changed from 1980 to 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Figure 17 showing regional comparisons.

claim: Percent difference in death rates between peak and minimum months did not change from 1980 to 2016 for ages ≥ 45 years.
source: In these ages, percent difference in death rates between peak and minimum months did not vary across climate regions, nor changed from 1980 to 2016.
evidence: This temporal stability is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 12.

claim: Seasonality of all-cause mortality largely disappeared after the 1990s in children under five years.
source: Under five years, seasonality of all-cause mortality largely disappeared after the 1990s.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figures 1 and 2 showing wavelet analysis for ages 0-4.

claim: In adolescents and young adults, especially males, death rates peaked in June/July and were lowest in December/January.
source: In adolescents and young adults, especially in males, death rates peaked in June/July and were lowest in December/January, driven by injury deaths.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 11 center of gravity analysis.

claim: Summer mortality peak in adolescents and young adults is driven by injury deaths.
source: In adolescents and young adults, especially in males, death rates peaked in June/July and were lowest in December/January, driven by injury deaths.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this causal relationship, supported by injury-specific analysis in Figure 7.

claim: There were 85,854,176 deaths in the USA from 1980 to 2016.
source: We used data on all 85,854,176 deaths in the USA from 1980 to 2016 from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS).
evidence: This is the total number of deaths analyzed, stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases make up nearly half of all deaths (48.1%).
source: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases make up nearly half of all deaths (48.1%), with most deaths in that group from cardiovascular diseases.
evidence: This percentage is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Most cardiorespiratory disease deaths are from cardiovascular diseases.
source: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases make up nearly half of all deaths (48.1%), with most deaths in that group from cardiovascular diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing 33,448,900 cardiovascular deaths out of 41,277,574 cardiorespiratory deaths.

claim: Deaths from cancers accounted for 23.2% of all deaths during the study period.
source: Next highest during the study period were deaths from cancers (23.2%), followed by injuries (6.8%), with two thirds of those being from unintentional injuries.
evidence: This percentage is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Deaths from injuries accounted for 6.8% of all deaths during the study period.
source: Next highest during the study period were deaths from cancers (23.2%), followed by injuries (6.8%), with two thirds of those being from unintentional injuries.
evidence: This percentage is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Two thirds of injury deaths were from unintentional injuries.
source: Next highest during the study period were deaths from cancers (23.2%), followed by injuries (6.8%), with two thirds of those being from unintentional injuries.
evidence: This proportion is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing 3,837,329 unintentional out of 5,803,046 total injury deaths.

claim: All-cause mortality in males had a 12 month seasonality in all age groups except ages 35–44 years.
source: All-cause mortality in males had a 12 month seasonality in all age groups, except ages 35–44 years, for whom there was periodicity at 6 months (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1 wavelet analysis.

claim: All-cause mortality in males aged 35-44 years had periodicity at 6 months.
source: All-cause mortality in males had a 12 month seasonality in all age groups, except ages 35–44 years, for whom there was periodicity at 6 months (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: In females, there was 12 month seasonality in all groups except 5–14 and 25–34 years.
source: In females, there was 12 month seasonality in all groups except 5–14 and 25–34 years (p-values=0.21 and 0.25, respectively) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Seasonality persisted throughout the entire analysis period in older ages.
source: While seasonality persisted throughout the entire analysis period in older ages, it largely disappeared after the late 1990s in children aged 0–4 years in both sexes and in women aged 15–24 years.
evidence: This temporal pattern is stated in the Results section and visible in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Seasonality largely disappeared after the late 1990s in children aged 0–4 years in both sexes.
source: While seasonality persisted throughout the entire analysis period in older ages, it largely disappeared after the late 1990s in children aged 0–4 years in both sexes and in women aged 15–24 years.
evidence: This temporal change is stated in the Results section and visible in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Seasonality largely disappeared after the late 1990s in women aged 15–24 years.
source: While seasonality persisted throughout the entire analysis period in older ages, it largely disappeared after the late 1990s in children aged 0–4 years in both sexes and in women aged 15–24 years.
evidence: This temporal change is stated in the Results section and visible in Figure 2.

claim: Deaths from all causes of death were seasonal in older adults (above 65 or 75 years depending on cause).
source: Deaths from all causes of death were seasonal in older adults (above 65 or 75 years depending on cause, p-values<0.06) (Figures 1–10 and respective figure supplements), except for intentional injuries and substance use disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with p-values and supported by multiple figures.

claim: Intentional injuries were not seasonal in older adults.
source: Deaths from all causes of death were seasonal in older adults (above 65 or 75 years depending on cause, p-values<0.06) (Figures 1–10 and respective figure supplements), except for intentional injuries and substance use disorders.
evidence: This exception is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substance use disorders were not seasonal in older adults.
source: Deaths from all causes of death were seasonal in older adults (above 65 or 75 years depending on cause, p-values<0.06) (Figures 1–10 and respective figure supplements), except for intentional injuries and substance use disorders.
evidence: This exception is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases exhibited seasonality throughout the life-course except for males aged 5–24 years and females aged 15–24 years.
source: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases, and within it respiratory infections, exhibited seasonality throughout the life-course (p-values<0.06) except for males aged 5–24 years and females aged 15–24 years (p-values>0.11).
evidence: This pattern is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Respiratory infections exhibited seasonality throughout the life-course except for males aged 5–24 years and females aged 15–24 years.
source: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases, and within it respiratory infections, exhibited seasonality throughout the life-course (p-values<0.06) except for males aged 5–24 years and females aged 15–24 years (p-values>0.11).
evidence: This pattern is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Injury deaths were seasonal from childhood through 44 years in women and through 64 years in men.
source: In addition to older ages, injury deaths were seasonal from childhood through 44 years in women and through 64 years in men (p-values<0.09).
evidence: This age-specific pattern is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Unintentional injuries drove the seasonality of injury deaths for females.
source: Unintentional injuries drove the seasonality of injury deaths for females, whereas both unintentional and intentional injuries were seasonal in males in most ages, with the exception of below 15 years and above 85 years when intentional injuries were not seasonal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This sex-specific pattern is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both unintentional and intentional injuries were seasonal in males in most ages.
source: Unintentional injuries drove the seasonality of injury deaths for females, whereas both unintentional and intentional injuries were seasonal in males in most ages, with the exception of below 15 years and above 85 years when intentional injuries were not seasonal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This sex-specific pattern is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intentional injuries were not seasonal in males below 15 years and above 85 years.
source: Unintentional injuries drove the seasonality of injury deaths for females, whereas both unintentional and intentional injuries were seasonal in males in most ages, with the exception of below 15 years and above 85 years when intentional injuries were not seasonal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This age-specific exception is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Consistent seasonality in cancer deaths only appeared after 55 years of age.
source: Consistent seasonality in cancer deaths (Figures 3,4) only appeared after 55 years of age (p-values<0.05).
evidence: This age threshold is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: No consistent seasonality was evident in substance use disorders.
source: No consistent seasonality was evident in substance use disorders (Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1) or maternal conditions (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This absence of seasonality is stated in the Results section and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: No consistent seasonality was evident in maternal conditions.
source: No consistent seasonality was evident in substance use disorders (Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1) or maternal conditions (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This absence of seasonality is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases were consistently highest in January and February and lowest in July and August across all ages.
source: Deaths from cardiorespiratory diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, chronic respiratory diseases and respiratory infections, were also consistently highest in January and February and lowest in July and August across all ages, except for chronic respiratory diseases in ages 5–24 years where there are few deaths from this cause leading to unstable estimates (p-values for seasonality from wavelet analysis ranged from 0.35 to 0.48 for these ages).
evidence: This temporal pattern is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 2.

claim: Among males aged 5–34 years, all-cause mortality peaked in June or July.
source: In contrast, among males aged 5–34 years, all-cause mortality peaked in June or July, as did deaths from injuries, which generally had a summer peak in males and females below 45 years of age.
evidence: This pattern is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Deaths from injuries generally had a summer peak in males and females below 45 years of age.
source: In contrast, among males aged 5–34 years, all-cause mortality peaked in June or July, as did deaths from injuries, which generally had a summer peak in males and females below 45 years of age.
evidence: This pattern is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 3.

claim: From 1980 to 2016, the proportional difference in all-cause death rates between peak and minimum months declined little for people older than 45 years of age (by less than eight percentage points).
source: From 1980 to 2016, the proportional (percent) difference in all-cause death rates between peak and minimum months declined little for people older than 45 years of age (by less than eight percentage points with p-values for declining trend >0.1) (Figure 12).
evidence: This temporal trend is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figure 12.

claim: The difference between peak (summer) and minimum (winter) death rates declined in younger ages by over 25 percentage points in males aged 5–14 years and 15–24 years.
source: In contrast, the difference between peak (summer) and minimum (winter) death rates declined in younger ages, by over 25 percentage points in males aged 5–14 years and 15–24 years (p-values<0.01), largely driven in the declining difference between summer and winter injury deaths.
evidence: This temporal change is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figure 12.

claim: The decline in seasonal mortality difference in young males was largely driven by declining difference between summer and winter injury deaths.
source: In contrast, the difference between peak (summer) and minimum (winter) death rates declined in younger ages, by over 25 percentage points in males aged 5–14 years and 15–24 years (p-values<0.01), largely driven in the declining difference between summer and winter injury deaths.
evidence: This causal relationship is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under five years of age, percent seasonal difference in all-cause death rates declined by 13 percentage points for boys but only five percentage points for girls.
source: Under five years of age, percent seasonal difference in all-cause death rates declined by 13 percentage points (p-value<0.01) for boys but only five percentage points (p-value=0.12) for girls.
evidence: This sex-specific difference is stated in the Results section with p-values and shown in Figure 12.

claim: Declines in seasonality of child deaths were a net effect of declining winter-summer difference in cardiorespiratory diseases deaths and increasing summer-winter difference in injury deaths.
source: These declines in seasonality of child deaths were a net effect of declining winter-summer difference in cardiorespiratory diseases deaths and increasing summer-winter difference in injury deaths, itself driven by increasing difference in non-intentional injuries (Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This explanation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: All-cause mortality peaks and minima in different climate regions are consistent with the national ones.
source: The subnational centre of gravity analysis showed that all-cause mortality peaks and minima in different climate regions are consistent with the national ones (Figures 13–16), indicating that seasonality is largely independent of geography.
evidence: This regional consistency is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 13-16.

claim: Seasonality is largely independent of geography.
source: The subnational centre of gravity analysis showed that all-cause mortality peaks and minima in different climate regions are consistent with the national ones (Figures 13–16), indicating that seasonality is largely independent of geography.
evidence: This inference is stated in the Results section based on the regional analysis shown in Figures 13-16.

claim: Above 45 years of age, there was little inter-region variation in the percent seasonal difference in all-cause mortality, despite large variation in temperature difference between peak and minimum months.
source: Furthermore, above 45 years of age, there was little inter-region variation in the percent seasonal difference in all-cause mortality, despite the large variation in temperature difference between the peak and minimum months (Figure 17).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 17.

claim: In men and women aged 65–74 years, all-cause mortality peaked in February in the Northeast and Southeast, even though the average temperatures for those regions were different by over 13 degrees Celsius.
source: For example, in men and women aged 65–74 years, all-cause mortality peaked in February in the Northeast and Southeast, even though the average temperatures for those regions were different by over 13 degrees Celsius (9.3 in the Southeast compared with −3.8 in the Northeast).
evidence: This specific example is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 13-14.

claim: Wavelets have been used to study the dynamics of weather phenomena.
source: Wavelets have been used to study the dynamics of weather phenomena (Moy et al., 2002) and infectious diseases (Grenfell et al., 2001).
evidence: This prior application is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: Wavelets have been used to study infectious diseases.
source: Wavelets have been used to study the dynamics of weather phenomena (Moy et al., 2002) and infectious diseases (Grenfell et al., 2001).
evidence: This prior application is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: A warmer world may lower winter mortality in temperate climates.
source: It has therefore been hypothesized that a warmer world may lower winter mortality in temperate climates (Langford and Bentham, 1995; Martens, 1998).
evidence: This hypothesis is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The seasonality of mortality may vary geographically due to geographical variations in mortality, localized weather patterns, and regional differences in adaptation measures.
source: In a large country like the USA, which possesses distinct climate regions, the seasonality of mortality may vary geographically, due to geographical variations in mortality, localized weather patterns, and regional differences in adaptation measures such as heating, air conditioning and healthcare (Davis et al., 2004; Braga et al., 2001; Kalkstein, 2013; Medina-Ramón and Schwartz, 2007).
evidence: This potential variation is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The presence and extent of seasonal variation in mortality may change over time.
source: The presence and extent of seasonal variation in mortality may also itself change over time (Bobb et al., 2014; Carson et al., 2006; Seretakis et al., 1997; Sheridan et al., 2009).
evidence: This temporal variability is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: Injuries accounted for 8% of all deaths in the USA in 1980.
source: Injuries, which accounted for 8% of all deaths in the USA in 1980 and 7.3% in 2016, may have seasonality that is distinct from so-called natural causes.
evidence: This percentage is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Injuries accounted for 7.3% of all deaths in the USA in 2016.
source: Injuries, which accounted for 8% of all deaths in the USA in 1980 and 7.3% in 2016, may have seasonality that is distinct from so-called natural causes.
evidence: This percentage is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Injuries may have seasonality that is distinct from so-called natural causes.
source: Injuries, which accounted for 8% of all deaths in the USA in 1980 and 7.3% in 2016, may have seasonality that is distinct from so-called natural causes.
evidence: This potential distinction is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by the results showing summer peaks for injuries versus winter peaks for other causes.

claim: The USA possesses nine distinct climate regions.
source: We also subdivided the national data geographically into nine climate regions used by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Figure 18 and Table 2) (Karl and Koss, 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation and shown in Figure 18 and Table 2.

claim: The Southeast and South are the hottest climate regions with average annual temperatures of 18.4°C and 18°C respectively.
source: On average, the Southeast and South are the hottest climate regions with average annual temperatures of 18.4°C and 18°C respectively; the South also possesses the highest average maximum monthly temperature (27.9°C in July).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Table 2.

claim: The South possesses the highest average maximum monthly temperature (27.9°C in July).
source: On average, the Southeast and South are the hottest climate regions with average annual temperatures of 18.4°C and 18°C respectively; the South also possesses the highest average maximum monthly temperature (27.9°C in July).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Southeast has the lowest variation in temperature throughout the year (an average range of 17.5°C).
source: The lowest variation in temperature throughout the year is that of the Southeast (an average range of 17.5°C).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The three coldest climate regions are West North Central, East North Central and the Northwest (7.6°C, 8.0°C, 8.2°C respectively).
source: The three coldest climate regions are West North Central, East North Central and the Northwest (7.6°C, 8.0°C, 8.2°C respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Table 2.

claim: The largest variation in temperature throughout the year is that of the coldest region, West North Central (an average range of 30.5°C).
source: Mirroring the characteristics of the hottest climate regions, the largest variation in temperature throughout the year is that of the coldest region, West North Central (an average range of 30.5°C), which also has the lowest average minimum monthly temperature (−6.5°C in January).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: West North Central has the lowest average minimum monthly temperature (−6.5°C in January).
source: Mirroring the characteristics of the hottest climate regions, the largest variation in temperature throughout the year is that of the coldest region, West North Central (an average range of 30.5°C), which also has the lowest average minimum monthly temperature (−6.5°C in January).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Northeast is the most populous region in the United States (with 19.8% total population in 2016).
source: The other climate regions, Northeast, Southwest, and Central, possess similar average temperatures (10°C to 14°C) and variation within the year of (23°C to 26°C), with the Northeast being the most populous region in the United States (with 19.8% total population in 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Table 2.

claim: The study identified distinct seasonal patterns in relation to age and sex, including higher all-cause summer mortality in young men.
source: We used wavelet and centre of gravity analyses, which allowed systematically identifying and characterizing seasonality of total and cause-specific mortality in the USA, and examining how seasonality has changed over time. We identified distinct seasonal patterns in relation to age and sex, including higher all-cause summer mortality in young men (Feinstein, 2002; Rau et al., 2018).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: All-cause and cause-specific mortality seasonality is largely similar in terms of both timing and magnitude across diverse climatic regions with substantially different summer and winter temperatures.
source: Importantly, we also showed that all-cause and cause-specific mortality seasonality is largely similar in terms of both timing and magnitude across diverse climatic regions with substantially different summer and winter temperatures.
evidence: This key finding is stated in the Discussion section and supported by Figures 13-17.

claim: A study of 36 cities in the USA found that excess mortality was not associated with seasonal temperature range.
source: A study of 36 cities in the USA, aggregated across age groups and over time, also found that excess mortality was not associated with seasonal temperature range (Kinney et al., 2015).
evidence: This prior finding is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: A European study found that the difference between winter and summer mortality was lower in colder Nordic countries than in warmer southern European nations.
source: In contrast, a European study found that the difference between winter and summer mortality was lower in colder Nordic countries than in warmer southern European nations (Healy, 2003; McKee, 1989) (the study's measure of temperature was mean annual temperature which differed from the temperature difference between maximum and minimum mortality used in our analysis although the two measures are correlated).
evidence: This contrasting finding is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The absence of variation in the magnitude of mortality seasonality indicates that different regions in the USA are similarly adapted to temperature seasonality.
source: The absence of variation in the magnitude of mortality seasonality indicates that different regions in the USA are similarly adapted to temperature seasonality, whereas Nordic countries may have better environmental (e.g. housing insulation and heating) and health system measures to counter the effects of cold winters than those in southern Europe.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: Nordic countries may have better environmental and health system measures to counter the effects of cold winters than those in southern Europe.
source: The absence of variation in the magnitude of mortality seasonality indicates that different regions in the USA are similarly adapted to temperature seasonality, whereas Nordic countries may have better environmental (e.g. housing insulation and heating) and health system measures to counter the effects of cold winters than those in southern Europe.
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section to explain differences between US and European findings.

claim: If the observed absence of association between the magnitude of mortality seasonality and seasonal temperature difference across climate regions persists over time, changes in temperature as a result of global climate change are unlikely to affect the winter-summer mortality difference.
source: If the observed absence of association between the magnitude of mortality seasonality and seasonal temperature difference across the climate regions also persists over time, the changes in temperature as a result of global climate change are unlikely to affect the winter-summer mortality difference.
evidence: This conditional prediction is stated in the Discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: The substantial decline in seasonal mortality differences in adolescents and young adults was related to the diminishing seasonality of (unintentional) injuries, especially from road traffic crashes.
source: The cause-specific analysis showed that the substantial decline in seasonal mortality differences in adolescents and young adults was related to the diminishing seasonality of (unintentional) injuries, especially from road traffic crashes, which are more likely to occur in the summer months (Liu et al., 2005) and are more common in men.
evidence: This explanation is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Road traffic crashes are more likely to occur in the summer months and are more common in men.
source: The cause-specific analysis showed that the substantial decline in seasonal mortality differences in adolescents and young adults was related to the diminishing seasonality of (unintentional) injuries, especially from road traffic crashes, which are more likely to occur in the summer months (Liu et al., 2005) and are more common in men.
evidence: This pattern is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: The weakening of seasonality in boys under five years of age was related to declining seasonality of death from cardiorespiratory diseases and increasing proportion of deaths from perinatal conditions.
source: The weakening of seasonality in boys under five years of age was related to two phenomena: first, the seasonality of death from cardiorespiratory diseases declined, and second, the proportion of deaths from perinatal conditions, which exhibit limited seasonality (Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and Figure 10—figure supplement 3), increased (MacDorman and Gregory, 2015).
evidence: This explanation is stated in the Discussion section with a citation and supported by referenced figures.

claim: Perinatal conditions exhibit limited seasonality.
source: The weakening of seasonality in boys under five years of age was related to two phenomena: first, the seasonality of death from cardiorespiratory diseases declined, and second, the proportion of deaths from perinatal conditions, which exhibit limited seasonality (Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and Figure 10—figure supplement 3), increased (MacDorman and Gregory, 2015).
evidence: This characteristic is stated in the Discussion section and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Mortality in older ages, where death rates are highest, maintained persistent seasonality over a period of three decades.
source: In contrast to young and middle ages, mortality in older ages, where death rates are highest, maintained persistent seasonality over a period of three decades (we note that although the percent seasonal difference in mortality has remained largely unchanged in these ages, the absolute difference in death rates between the peak and minimum months has declined because total mortality has a declining long-term trend).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Discussion section and supported by Figures 1, 2, and 12.

claim: Although the percent seasonal difference in mortality has remained largely unchanged in older ages, the absolute difference in death rates between the peak and minimum months has declined because total mortality has a declining long-term trend.
source: In contrast to young and middle ages, mortality in older ages, where death rates are highest, maintained persistent seasonality over a period of three decades (we note that although the percent seasonal difference in mortality has remained largely unchanged in these ages, the absolute difference in death rates between the peak and minimum months has declined because total mortality has a declining long-term trend).
evidence: This clarification is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Environmental and health service interventions are needed for older populations irrespective of geography and local climate.
source: This finding demonstrates the need for environmental and health service interventions targeted towards this group irrespective of geography and local climate.
evidence: This recommendation is stated in the Discussion section based on the persistent seasonality in older ages.

claim: Examples of interventions include enhancing the availability of environmental and medical protective factors, such as better insulation of homes, winter heating provision and flu vaccinations, for the vulnerable older population.
source: Examples of such interventions include enhancing the availability of both environmental and medical protective factors, such as better insulation of homes, winter heating provision and flu vaccinations, for the vulnerable older population (Katiyo et al., 2017).
evidence: These intervention examples are stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Social interventions, including regular visits to the isolated elderly during peak mortality periods, are important to protect vulnerable groups.
source: Social interventions, including regular visits to the isolated elderly during peak mortality periods to ensure that they are optimally prepared for adverse conditions, and responsive and high-quality emergency care, are also important to protect this vulnerable group (Healy, 2003; Lerchl, 1998; Katiyo et al., 2017).
evidence: These intervention examples are stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Emergent new technologies, such as always-connected hands-free communications devices, in-house cameras, and personal sensors provide an opportunity to enhance care for older, more vulnerable groups.
source: Emergent new technologies, such as always-connected hands-free communications devices with the outside world, in-house cameras, and personal sensors also provide an opportunity to enhance care for the older, more vulnerable groups in the population, especially in winter when the elderly have fewer social interactions (Morris, 2013).
evidence: This opportunity is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Such interventions are important today, and will remain so as the population ages and climate change increases the within- and between-season weather variability.
source: Such interventions are important today, and will remain so as the population ages and climate change increases the within- and between-season weather variability.
evidence: This forward-looking statement is made in the Discussion section.

claim: A limitation of the study is that it did not investigate seasonality of mortality by socioeconomic characteristics.
source: A limitation of our study is that we did not investigate seasonality of mortality by socioeconomic characteristics which may help with understanding its determinants and planning responses.
evidence: This limitation is explicitly stated in the Strengths and limitations section.

claim: Investigating seasonality by socioeconomic characteristics may help with understanding its determinants and planning responses.
source: A limitation of our study is that we did not investigate seasonality of mortality by socioeconomic characteristics which may help with understanding its determinants and planning responses.
evidence: This potential benefit is stated in the Strengths and limitations section.

claim: The study used geo-coded mortality data and wavelets to analyse the seasonality of mortality by age group and sex from 1980 to 2016 in the USA and its subnational climatic regions.
source: We used geo-coded mortality data and wavelets to analyse the seasonality of mortality by age group and sex from 1980 to 2016 in the USA and its subnational climatic regions.
evidence: This methodological approach is stated in the Abstract.

claim: The study used centre of gravity analysis and circular statistics methods to understand the timing of maximum and minimum mortality.
source: We also used centre of gravity analysis and circular statistics methods to understand the timing of maximum and minimum mortality.
evidence: This methodological approach is stated in the Introduction.

claim: Wavelet analysis uncovers the presence and frequency of repeated maxima and minima in each age-sex-specific death rate time series.
source: We used wavelet analysis to investigate seasonality for each age-sex group. Wavelet analysis uncovers the presence, and frequency, of repeated maxima and minima in each age-sex-specific death rate time series (Hubbard, 1998; Torrence and Compo, 1998).
evidence: This description of wavelet analysis is stated in the Materials and methods section with citations.

claim: The study used the R package WaveletComp (version 1.0) for the wavelet analysis.
source: We used the R package WaveletComp (version 1.0) for the wavelet analysis.
evidence: This software tool is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study used the R package CircStats (version 0.2.4) for circular statistics analysis.
source: The R package CircStats (version 0.2.4) was used for this analysis.
evidence: This software tool is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Temperature data was obtained from ERA-Interim.
source: We obtained data on temperature from ERA-Interim, which combines predictions from a physical model with ground-based and satellite measurements (Dee et al., 2011).

claim: ERA-Interim combines predictions from a physical model with ground-based and satellite measurements.
